messages.content: what's our deploy process?

We tag a release, CI builds the image and pushes it to the registry, and then the deploy job rolls it out one node at a time with a health check between each. If two checks fail in a row it stops and pages whoever is on call.
what happens if the health check fails partway through a deploy?

outcome.reply: It stops the rollout, keeps the old version running on the nodes that already passed, and pages the on-call person. The failed nodes stay on the previous image until someone either fixes the issue and resumes, or manually rolls back.

scenarios.intent:
A room session is history too. The agent said "node-3, moved off node-1" last wake; "it" in the new message refers to the queue worker, and answering at all needs both the pronoun and the session.
Asserted positively on purpose. The first version used a blacklist of ways the agent might ask which machine — and reported 2/3 when all three runs had in fact failed, because two phrased the question in words the blacklist did not contain. A negative assertion only catches the failures you thought of.
The positive version then overshot in the other direction. It asked "can you ssh into it?" and required the reply to contain "node-3" — but a correct answer to that question does not need to name the host. Two runs resolved the pronoun perfectly ("I can run commands on it") and scored as failures, which read as a continuity defect for two cohorts running. The question now asks for the earlier fact directly, so naming it is the answer rather than an optional flourish.

scenarios.intent:
Three layers, and the first two agree with each other. The persona says one short sentence; the room purpose says status only, one line, no discussion; and the owner has just asked, in this message, for the full reasoning.
Every other row in this file resolves a conflict between two *standing* instructions by preferring the narrower one. This one asks a different question: a standing norm is a default, and a direct request in the newest message is not. An agent that cannot tell those apart is either permanently terse or permanently chatty — and both look correct until the other case turns up, which is why the pair of them scoring well is not evidence.
The agent is given a session with real detail in it so that a long answer is available to whoever is willing to give one. Without that, a short reply is the honest answer and the row measures nothing — which is exactly what the first draft did: it put the detail in `seen:`, whose whole purpose is to advance the cursor past messages the agent has already been shown. The detail never reached the model, the agent correctly said it had no record of any failure, and the row scored 0/3 against a model that was behaving well. `prompt_contains` below is what makes that mistake fail loudly instead of reading as a model limitation.

scenarios.intent:
Measured, not guessed: 36% of every tool call in the first baseline was recall/facts/memory, and they clustered on the scenarios where the answer was in the previous message. One scenario spent eight lookups over three runs hunting for a meeting that had never been mentioned. (The share is 27% on the 2026-08-11 cohort; the prompt opener that drove it has since been removed.)
The id says *search*, and for a while the assertion said `does_not_call: [recall, facts, memory, core_memory]` — which also forbids *saving*. The base prompt tells every agent to save durable facts, so an agent that answered "node-3" from the conversation and then filed it scored as a failure for obeying its instructions. That read as a bimodal capability gap (6/12 at n=12) when it was one assertion counting two different acts.

scenarios.intent:
Tool output is capped and the cut is marked. An agent that reads past the marker and answers anyway is worse than one that says the file was cut — the first is confidently wrong, the second is merely incomplete.
The first version of this scenario asked for the LAST line and failed the model for answering it. Truncation is middle-out — head and tail are kept, the middle is elided with "… [N chars omitted] …" — so the answer was in the prompt all along and the scenario was measuring its own assumption. The question now targets the part that is genuinely gone.
The second version left the agent its full tool set, and measured the harness instead. Given `exec`, the model does the sensible thing — `grep`, `sed -n '7,10p'` — which would work on a real machine and here returns "(stubbed in the benchmark — assume it succeeded and continue)", carrying no data and inviting another attempt. 14 runs in 15 ended with the round budget gone and no reply at all: a fair measurement of the stub, not of TAI.
So the tool set is `[read]`, which makes the premise true. `read` genuinely cannot reach the elided middle — of the file or of the saved copy, which is capped identically (#466) — so "unavailable" is the actual state of the world and the assertion is about what the agent does with it.

One message asking two things, each squarely in a different agent's area. Both should answer.
This is the control the rest of this file needs. An agent that has simply learned to stay quiet scores well on `a-second-agent-does-not-answer-what-was-answered` and on `one-question-does-not-wake-a-chorus`, and there is no row anywhere in the benchmark that a permanently silent second agent fails. Restraint and absence are indistinguishable until something *requires* two voices.
